name: Det. Vincent Lamarque
languages: French (his father insisted, and his grandmother spoke nothing else)
equipment: Heavy overcoat, black cashmere, his father's, too good for a policeman and everyone at the precinct says so
.38 revolver (Smith & Wesson Military & Police, department issue), 6 rounds loaded, in a belt holster
Nightstick, which he leaves in the car more often than he should
Badge and warrant card, New Orleans Police Department, Detective, 5th District
A Carnival invitation, engraved, to the ball of the Krewe of Oneiros at the Municipal Auditorium on Mardi Gras night, addressed to Mr. and Mrs. Gaston Lamarque and Family
His Marine Corps discharge, folded inside his badge case behind his mother's photograph
features: Doors Open (Old Money origin: doormen, club secretaries and private secretaries let him through unless told not to; advantage on Society checks among the wealthy; disadvantage on Streetwise checks below the tracks until he has spent a scene showing he can be trusted)

The Badge (Cop: lawful authority to enter a crime scene, demand identification, commandeer a telephone or car and detain a person for questioning; advantage on Intimidation and Persuasion against anyone who respects the law. The badge has a chain of command: Captain Lebeau can give him orders, and using it for something his superiors have not sanctioned raises Heat by 1. People who will not talk to cops will not talk to him: disadvantage on Streetwise with them unless they do not know)
Academy Training: Riot Squad (Cop: +1 AC while wearing medium armor, not counted in his overcoat AC; he can shove a creature as a bonus action when he takes the Attack action)
Collar (Cop, 2nd level: when he hits with a melee attack, a bonus action to grapple; he can cuff a grappled creature as an action with no check, and a cuffed creature has disadvantage to escape)

Assignment: Detective (Cop, 3rd level: proficient in Forensics; once per long rest, examining a scene, the GM tells him which of the people he knows had the best opportunity, though not necessarily the motive)

Old Outfit (Veteran background: in any legion post or bar with a flag over the register he can get a meal, a bed, a job lead or a quiet word about a man who served; he reads rank and bearing at a glance)

personality.traits: I am courteous to everyone, which my captain calls insolence and my father calls breeding. I take notes in French so the squad room cannot read them. I do not raise my voice; I lower it.
personality.ideals: The law is supposed to be the same on Esplanade Avenue as it is on Jourdan Avenue. I know it is not. I joined to find out whether one man can make it a little more so.
personality.bonds: My mother, who is ill, and my father, Gaston Lamarque, a cotton factor and a lieutenant of the Krewe of Oneiros, who got me my detective's badge with one telephone call and has not let me forget it. The Marines of my company, who were from places like Ohio and Alabama and Brooklyn and did not care who my family was.
personality.flaws: I have spent my whole life being told what a Lamarque does and does not do, and I still, at thirty-four, cannot quite disobey my father to his face. And I have been a detective for six weeks; I am more afraid of being a fool than of being wrong.

appearance: A tall, slim, dark-haired man of thirty-four with an old-family face, long, sallow and handsome, a thin scar along his jaw from Okinawa, and very correct manners. He wears his father's black cashmere overcoat over a department-store suit and looks like a man dressed for two different lives at once.
backstory: Vincent Lamarque was born on Esplanade Avenue in a house with a carriage gate, a courtyard and a portrait of a great-great-grandfather who came from Bordeaux with nothing and died with a sugar plantation, and he was raised to be a cotton factor like his father and grandfather, a member of the right clubs and a lieutenant in the Krewe of Oneiros. Instead, in 1941, he joined the Marine Corps as a private, out of a stubbornness his mother says he gets from her side, and he came home in 1945 a sergeant with a scar and no interest in cotton. He wanted to be a police officer. His father, appalled, made one telephone call to a man he rides with in the krewe, and Vincent found himself a detective in the 5th District, which covers the Ninth Ward and the Industrial Canal, under Captain Achille Lebeau, who does not like being telephoned about his detectives by cotton factors. On Friday morning, 1 March, at a quarter past eight, Vincent catches the body at the Industrial Canal lock. By noon, before the coroner has finished, Captain Lebeau tells him the case is an accidental drowning of an intoxicated man and that he is to type it up that way. Vincent has typed it up. He has not yet signed it.
